samples.text:
The diagram shows the stages of how coal is formed. There are eight stages, from the swamp forest to the mining of coal.

In the first stage, plants grow in warm wetlands, which is called swamp forest. Then the plants die and they fall into the water, but they do not decay fully. After that, the layers of dead plants build up and they are compressed, and this become peat.

Next, the peat is covered by sand and mud and this take millions of years. Then the heat and the pressure remove the water from it, so it change into lignite. After more compression, it becomes bituminous coal, which has more carbon than before.

In the seventh stage, the coal become anthracite. This is the hardest coal and it has about 90% of carbon. Finally, people extract the coal from underground seams by mining, so it can be used.

Overall, the process is very long and it starts with living plants and ends with hard coal which is mined from under the ground. The coal has more carbon in the later stages of the process.
samples.why: Overview placed at the end · all stages covered in sequence with the key figure · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · repeated agreement errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The diagram illustrates how coal is formed over time, beginning with plants in swamp forests and ending with the extraction of coal from the ground.

Overall, there are eight stages in the process, which takes millions of years. As the material is buried and compressed, it gradually changes from peat into different types of coal, with the later types containing more carbon.

In the first stage, plants grow in warm wetlands. When they die, they fall into the water, where they do not decay completely. Over time, layers of this plant debris build up and are compressed to form peat, which is then buried under sand and mud over millions of years.

As a result of heat and pressure, the water is removed and the peat turns into lignite. Further compression produces bituminous coal, which has a higher carbon content, and eventually anthracite are formed. This is the hardest type of coal and it is made up of about 90% carbon. In the final stage, the coal is mined from underground seams, which is the only part of the process carried out by people.
samples.why: Clear overview of timescale and main change · logical progression with cause and sequence linkers · good topic vocabulary (debris, compressed, carbon content) · mostly error-free with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The diagram outlines the natural process by which coal is formed and the point at which it is finally extracted by humans for use.

It is clear that coal formation is an extremely slow, eight-stage process spanning millions of years, during which buried plant matter is progressively compressed into increasingly carbon-rich forms of coal, culminating in anthracite. Only the last stage involves human activity.

The sequence starts in warm, swampy wetlands, where plants flourish. When these plants die, they fall into the water and, crucially, fail to decompose fully, so that successive layers of debris accumulate and are compressed into peat. Over millions of years, this peat is buried beneath deposits of sand and mud.

Heat and pressure then drive out the water, converting the compressed peat into lignite, the first of the three types of coal shown. With further compression, lignite becomes bituminous coal, which has a higher carbon content, and ultimately anthracite, the hardest variety, containing approximately 90% carbon. At the final stage, this coal is extracted by mining underground seams, marking the shift from a natural process to a human one.
samples.why: Well-placed overview capturing timescale and progression · stages selected and linked skilfully · precise vocabulary (accumulate, drive out, variety) · wide range of structures · error-free.
